title: 5 habits for improving at chess
summary: Want to improve at chess? Build these 5 beginner-friendly habits to sharpen your skills, learn from mistakes, and get more from every game.
body_markdown:
Improving at chess can sound daunting, especially if you’re just starting out. The game is so complex that[even computers aren’t close to solving it](https://blog.duolingo.com/chess-computers-vs-humans/) . But there’s good news: Beginners often make some of the fastest progress!


Here are 5 tips to help jump-start your chess journey.


## Find a community 👥


Chess is a social game, and connecting with like-minded people who share your passion can deepen your understanding, keep you motivated, and even lead to new friendships.


Look for chess meetups in your area, join a local club, or try a tournament if you’re eager to compete. Playing and analyzing with others—especially stronger players—can quickly boost your chess knowledge.


If meeting in person isn’t an option, there are plenty of online communities, too. You could also convince a friend to learn with you so you can play and improve together!


## Play, play, play ♟️


Whether[online](https://preview.duolingo.com/chess?ref=blog.duolingo.com) or over a real board, chess is meant to be played! It may feel stressful at first, but the thrill of trying to outwit an opponent is unmatched.


And don’t worry about losing. Even[the very best players](https://blog.duolingo.com/how-to-become-a-chess-grandmaster/) have been defeated more times than they can count. A loss[you can learn from](https://blog.duolingo.com/chess-game-review/) is infinitely better than not playing!


## Analyze your games **🔍**


Just because a game ends doesn’t mean your learning does. Take a few minutes to review what happened: What went well? Where could you improve? Did you miss an opportunity or a threat?


You can analyze the game with your opponent, a friend, or Duolingo’s very own[Chess Game Review](https://blog.duolingo.com/chess-game-review/) ! Regardless of the method, try to actively understand where you went wrong and why. This may feel painful after a loss, but mistakes are an essential part of improving. Everyone makes them, and the best way to avoid repeating them is to learn from them.


## Solve chess puzzles 🧩


One of the easiest ways to train between games is by solving puzzles, and thankfully, it’s also a lot of fun! Just a few minutes of puzzles each day will strengthen your ability to recognize common tactical patterns, such as[forks](https://blog.duolingo.com/beginner-chess-terms/#fork) and[pins](https://blog.duolingo.com/beginner-chess-terms/#pin) . Before long, you’ll start spotting these patterns in your own games and using them to outsmart your opponents.


You’ll get some puzzles wrong, and that’s a good thing! When that happens, pause and take a moment to understand *why* your attempt didn’t work. Every chess puzzle you mess up is a valuable learning opportunity.


## Make use of other resources 📚


People have been writing about chess for hundreds of years, so there’s no shortage of books to explore. Whether you want[a beginner-friendly overview](https://blog.duolingo.com/chess-pieces-names/) of basic strategies or an in-depth guide to a particular[opening](https://blog.duolingo.com/popular-chess-openings/) or endgame, there’s a resource out there for you.


[Educational chess videos](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC7zYqA6IG4pg-PllrkQiO2Q?ref=blog.duolingo.com) are also widely available. You can watch experts explain grandmaster games, break down certain patterns, or talk through their moves as they play. You’ll learn the most when you actively think along, but even watching for fun can help you pick up a useful tip or two for your own games!

## Keep playing, keep learning


Books, videos, puzzles, and games can teach you a great deal about chess,[its culture](https://blog.duolingo.com/chess-slang/) , and its history. Stay curious, keep practicing, and see where your next move takes you!
